title: Podcast hosting
brief: You host shows for creators. Listeners press play and download big audio files, and creators upload a new episode now and then. The audio is the bill: every episode downloaded costs bandwidth.

clarify.q: How often does an episode change?
clarify.a: Never after it is published. Audio files are the same for everyone, so copies are safe.

clarify.q: Do listeners all arrive at the same time?
clarify.a: Mostly in the morning commute. But a famous guest can send a huge crowd at once.
No. A few thousand a day across all shows. Uploads are few and can take a few seconds.

clarify.q: What matters most to the creator?
clarify.a: That the episode plays, and that the hosting bill leaves them something to keep.

notes: An average episode is about 50 MB (approx.). The game groups it into 2 MB stream chunks.

hints: Where does the money go in a service that sends big files? Think about what you pay per gigabyte sent.
Episodes never change, so a CDN can hold them. Fewer trips to your own storage means a lower bill and a faster start.
Try: listeners -> CDN -> object storage for the audio. Add one small API for show pages and uploads. You do not need many servers here.

editorial.summary: Podcast hosting is a bandwidth business. The files are large, identical for everyone, and never change. Put the audio in object storage, put a CDN in front, and keep the servers tiny. The famous-guest crowd then costs almost nothing extra at the origin.

designs.name: CDN straight to object storage
designs.why: The CDN reads audio from object storage and keeps it. A small API fleet handles show pages and uploads. There is nothing big to scale because the heavy part is the CDN.

tradeoffs: A very long cache time keeps the CDN bill down, but a creator who replaces an episode must wait or rename the file.
Collapsing misses means ten thousand people asking for a brand-new episode produce one request to storage, not ten thousand.
Two small servers in two zones cost little more than one and survive a building failure.
Cheaper bandwidth from a bigger CDN contract needs a commitment. A small host pays list price.
editorial.realWorld: A popular episode is downloaded within hours of release by most of its audience, so a cache filled by the first few listeners serves almost everyone else. Typical CDN prices are around 2 to 8 cents per GB (approx.).
